title: The northern share of M3+ events fell from 72 to 47 percent in an Oklahoma box in 2021-2025
abstract: We test whether residual Oklahoma activity has the same broad spatial shares as peak activity. In an OGS box, the share of M3+ events north of 36 degrees N fell from 1511/2092 in 2014-2016 to 43/92 in 2021-2025. The north-to-south retention ratio is 0.337, with a year-bootstrap percentile range of 0.192-0.569. ComCat gives 0.331 but shares source data. We derive a sharp bound for a nonnegative mixture of a fixed peak spatial pattern, the historical background mean and an arbitrary remainder. If counts equal means, at least 29.1 percent of late activity lies outside the first two components. Even if all historical background is placed in the south, the bound is 27.0 percent. A background at least 4.28 times the observed historical rate is needed to remove that bound. The result is exploratory. Only three peak years are available; year exchangeability is uncertain. The contrast weakens at M3.5+ and after removal of the Prague area. This constrains spatial rate models but does not identify a driver, prove new fault activation or test the ETAS taper. We supply aggregate evidence, code, source hashes and 1000 independent optimization checks. Raw catalogs remain external.

display.caption: The northern share and north-to-south retention ratio decrease. Error bars use whole-year bootstrap draws. The right panel gives the sharp component bound when counts equal means. The model does not identify earthquake causes.
